rhythms.d: Abioueka (Abiweika, Abiouka) is a Sousou-dance for young children.

Adjos is a rhythm of the Baolé-people from the South of Ivory Coast. It’s a slow and majestic dance to be played for the king. Nowadays it’s played much faster. According to Baba Toure the song below was sung especially in honour of Samore Touré (a very important but cruel King).

Abondan (Abonda, Abondant) is a rhythm from the Baoulé-people from the Ivory Coast. It is probably a very old rhythm that was played when the King went out to ride (on the horse). The story goes that boys and girls danced in honour of the King. Then the King held a speech. Nowadays danced in circle.

Bada (Badan, Badagbe) is a Dunumba-rhythm from the Malinke, that is played as a transition between two other dunumba’s. It has a complete other rhythm compared to other dunumba’s. During the dance it offers the people that – in their enthusiasm – have closed to much on the drummers and each other , the opportunity to enlarge the circle around the players. A musical phrase from Guinea used to signal the ensemble and crowd to enlarge the circle. This is used when the crowd has encroached upon the drummers, making it difficult to play.
A rhythm from Guinea, from the Malinke. Mask of the porcupine (bala).
From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian.

A rhythm from Guinea also played for circumcision festivals where women are allowed to dance the movements of the rhythm Soli. It originates from the village of Balan, located in the region of Kouroussa.“Balan” is a village near Kouroussa, “sondé” means thief. The inhabitants of the village are called thiefs in the song that goes with this rhythm (teasing). The rhythm is an exception within the Dunumba-rhythm-family. Both men and women dance. While the men are dancing dunumba-steps, the woman are dancing the söli-steps.)

A rhythm from Guinea also played for circumcision festivals where women are allowed to dance the movements of the rhythm Soli. It originates from the village of Balan, located in the region of Kouroussa.“Balan” is a village near Kouroussa, “sondé” means thief. The inhabitants of the village are called thiefs in the song that goes with this rhythm (teasing). The rhythm is an exception within the Dunumba-rhythm-family. Both men and women dance. While the men are dancing dunumba-steps, the woman are dancing the söli-steps.
A rhythm from a Dutchman

From Guinea. Played in honor of the goddess Koudaba to insure the success of the village. It is a Dunumba-rhythm from the Malinke in the Hamana-region in Guinea and one of the Dunumba-dances of the strong men from Hamana (Kouroussa, Northern Guinee). It is also known as Bando Djeï. Bandogialli is the name of some kind of ape-family (Bando Djeï) with a white tail. The baranti dancers have a ring around their neck with white hair, crests or ‘sheep-beards’ attached to it, that remember to the white tail of the ape. As the shoulders of the dancer move up and down the white sheep-beard seesaws along.
A rhythm from the Malinke in Guinea. About the woman who rejects the man.
A rhythm from the Malinke in Guinea. There are two kinds of the Baobap tree in West-Africa: The Seda and the Bannan. Körö means ‘under’ (the tree).

A rhythm originating from South-Mali. Dance of the ‘nobel’ people. Once a year a great feast is held at the village. The king comes to the village for this occasion. Nowadays also at mariages and other party’s.

A rhythm originating from South-Mali. Dance of the ‘nobel’ people. Once a year a great feast is held at the village. The king comes to the village for this occasion. Nowadays also at mariages and other party’s.

A rhythm originating from South-Mali. Dance of the ‘nobel’ people. Once a year a great feast is held at the village. The king comes to the village for this occasion. Nowadays also at mariages and other party’s.
A Dunumba from Guinea. When a festival is about to begin in the large village square (Bara Duu), the drummers play this rhythm, to gather the villagers together.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
by WAP pages
A Malinke-rhythm called after the instrument with this name. In the tradition it is played without a Sangban.

Not a traditional rhythm from Guinea. It is based on a rhythm played on the instrument (M’)Bolon. It is an instrument made of a calabash, with a stick mounted on it and holding 3 (or 4) strings. It is usually used as a bass accompany in melodic pieces.
Bolowi is an adaptation of a melody originally played on the Bolon by the Senufo from the Korhogo region.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
Harouna Dembele by <a href='https://www.facebook.com/yeelenathens/' onclick='stefanoClick()' target='_blank'>Stefano Fratini Attanasio

From Guinea, is a rhythm honoring the women fishers. Traditionally only men are allowed to use fishing boats so dalah is played to protect the women from the many dangers they face standing in the open waters.
A rhythm from a Dutchman.
A hunters song song from the Malinke area in Guinea.

From Guinea. Damba is a Malinke pre-marriage rhythm played on the occasion of the bride’s ritual bath before the marriage ceremony. ‘Dunumba’ rhythms are primarily danced by men as a display of strength and beauty. Damba is traditionally played for a young woman preparing for marriage.
Originally coming from the Kassounke-people from Southern Mali (Kayes-region), it was a competition dance for the young men. Nowadays is a popular rhythm, played all over West Africa.

From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. Originally coming from the Kassounke-people from Southern Mali (Kayes-region), it was a competition dance for the young men. Nowadays is a popular rhythm, played all over West Africa.

From Guinea. This doundoumba is danced by young girls. It is a lighthearted exchange of mockery between the girls and the drummers. The drummers tease the girls with gestures of a sexual nature and the girls respond by obviously doubting the drummers playing abilities.

This rhythm from Guinea (Kankan-area) is played to introduce the Mendiani dancers prior to the Mendiani. The dancers are carried out to the Bara, a community space in the village, on the shoulders of men. They pay their respects to the drummers as the are carried around the Bara.
A rhythm from Burkina Faso and means dance of the mothers. A friend of the mother organises this for the daughter.

Diansa is a very popular rhythm originating from the Kayes region in Mali. It is performed in the evening for most celebrations, I.E. full moon, Spring, Summer and Winter solstice, weddings and harvest celebrations.

Diansa is a very popular rhythm originating from the Kayes region in Mali. It is performed in the evening for most celebrations, I.E. full moon, Spring, Summer and Winter solstice, weddings and harvest celebrations.

From Malinke region. This is one of the many rhythms played for the farmers. Dibon is a couple of birds; male and female. During daytime they are together but at night they each find their own tree to sleep in. In the morning, as they want to join, one sings and the other responds while flying to the first.

Originating from Mali's Sikasso region, Didadi is played for the expected arrival of an important person or at end-of-the-year holidays. It is an easily dance able rhythm where everyone is free to dance his or her own interpretation. T

Djaa is a Malinke-rhythm that – like many rhythms – originates from the handclapping by woman. It´s a dance of seduction where young men and woman dance in two half-circles in front of each other. It is often the climax of a party where men and woman dance.
Djaa Kouroussa is the Djaa from the Kouroussa region.
Djaa Siguiri is the Djaa from the Siguiri region.

From Guinea. In Wassolon this is a welcoming rhythm. The name of the rhythm Djabara (Yabara) comes from the music-instrument Djabara. It’s from the Wassolon-region and is a rhythm of greeting of (high positioned) guests of the village. During the ‘french’ period it was urged to play this rhythm for french government officials.
A rhythm from the Cassamance area in the southern part of Senegal. It usually played on the Serouba drums. It is very popular with weddings or ‘name-giving-day’ (one week after birth).
A rhythm from the Wassolon people of Guinea. It is played at the end of Ramadan.

From Mali. Djelidon, Djelifoli, Lamba or Sanja (the last one means Happy New Year in the Bambara language) are all designations for dance, that was traditionally performed by the djeli, the griot (don is dance). It was accompanied by the balafon or kora. Nowadays more drums are used and also played by the djembé ensemble.

From Guinea. Played during the circumcision festivities, it is a tribute to the ones who carry out the circumcisions.

A rhythm from the people located in the lower southeast region of Mali, near the border of Burkina Faso. It is played for and by the caste of indentured servants who served the Royal courts of Mandeng chiefs and royal families in ancient times. The dance was a show of family pride and solidarity.
From Sierrra Leone. A mask dance from the Temine people that is traditionally played on a square frame drum called a sikko. It has been adapted to djembe and is very popular in Guinea.

From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. From Sierrra Leone. A mask dance from the Temine people that is traditionally played on a square frame drum called a sikko. It has been adapted to djembe and is very popular in Guinea.

From Guinea. It means Great Dancer and is played to honor Maria Magbwe, a dancer from Famadou Kante's village.
A rhythm of hunting
From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. From Guinea. This is the oldest Doundoumba and is commonly referred to as the mother of all Doundoumba's
From Guinea. This is the oldest Doundoumba and is commonly referred to as the mother of all Doundoumba's
A very old forerunner of the Dunumba rhythms that was played in his native village of Kato in Senegal.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
A welcoming rhythm from Guinea

A rhythm from Guinea used for non-ritualistic celebrations such as welcoming celebrations. In the area of Mandiana it’s played as important people come to the village incidentally also played during full moon ceremonies. Also often heard during weddings baptisms and many other festivities. Fankani is dance for women.

From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. A rhythm from Guinea used for non-ritualistic celebrations such as welcoming celebrations. Fankani is dance for women.

by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
A rhythm that is traditionally played by the blacksmiths of Northern Ivory Coast (especially the villages Korhoga, Mandially and Sinematjalli).
A rhythm from Mali played to honor the shoemakers' caste. Garankefoli is the name of the rhythm, Garankedon is the name of the dance. The dance used to be danced by women.

A Malinke dance for women. It comes from the Hamana area in Guinea and is played on many occasions. It is an individually danced dance. The solo dancer jumps into a circle of people and dances a short solo.

It is a rhythm for young people. A young man is chosen, this is allowed dancing with the young girls. Gumbé is played at special occasions. Also played at the tabaski festival (Islamic sacrifice festival).
The movements of this dance from Guinea express a fight between the dancers, referring back to the days of settling disputes with the Doundoumba.
This rhythm from Guinea gets its name from a prefect in the region of Hamanah.

An old rhythm from Guinea. Like many old rhythms in West Africa, these are almost always originated in women’s groups, who together made hadclapping and sang rhythms. Hakili literally means ‘Good spirit’. The song calls to fill in your life and to act from a “good spirit.” Life is short; you better make something beautiful out of it and act with a good heart towards others.

A doundounba from Guinea created for modern use by the ballet. The dunumba-rhythms are traditionally only danced by men: ‘The dance of the strong men’. The Kadan is a dance for the bilakoros (non-circumcised children). The bilakoros are the specialists in this dance, which people come and watch like a show.

The Kakilambé is a masked figure from Guinea, which protects the forest. It is said that only the initiated dancer may see the Kakilambé. The masked figure emerges from the forest and converses with the initiated one, telling him what needs to be done for the survival and safety of the forest and the village.

From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. The Kakilambé is a masked figure from Guinea, which protects the forest. It is said that only the initiated dancer may see the Kakilambé. The masked figure emerges from the forest and converses with the initiated one, telling him what needs to be done for the survival and safety of the forest and the village.

A rhythm composed by Famoudou Konate. Kamerenen Dönna is called the young man who is gifted with special dancing skills.
A rhythm composed by Famoudou Konate. Kamerenen Dönna is called the young man who is gifted with special dancing skills.

From Guinea. A rhythm associated with the Mendiani celebration, sometimes played with Denadon. Kanin means friendship and is a Malinke-rhythm created by Mamady Keïta during when he was the artistic leader of the National Ballet de Guinea.

A rhythm of the Malinke people in East Guinea played while the workers harvest the fields. The word means granary. The workers may have to walk miles from field to field and kassa is sometimes played while the workers walk to the next field. It is also played to celebrate a bountiful harvest at a festival, called the Kassaladon, which takes place after the harvest.

From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. A rhythm of the Malinke people in East Guinea played while the workers harvest the fields. The word means granary. The workers may have to walk miles from field to field and kassa is sometimes played while the workers walk to the next field. It is also played to celebrate a bountiful harvest at a festival, called the Kassaladon, which takes place after the harvest.
It’s a rhythm that is part of the Kassa family, that support the farmers during their work. From east Guinea.
It’s a rhythm that is part of the Kassa family, that support the farmers during their work. From east Guinea.
It’s a rhythm that is part of the Kassa family, that support the farmers during their work. From east Guinea.

Originates from the Faranah region in Guinea, it is a rhythm of the medicine man, and it is played during circumcision to protect the young initiates from evil spirits. The Kawa is a mask who tracks down wizards and other people of the shadow, marabous or evil sorcerers of the fetish cult. He is armed with the börö, a sack that allows him both to detect and to strike them. His task is nevertheless difficult, for the wizards defend themselves. As is the case with most of the malinké maskers, the Kawa is exclusively masculine and dances alone, accompanied by the singing and the handclapping of the women.
Originates from the Faranah region in Guinea , it is a rhythm of the medicine man, and it is played during circumcision to protect the young initiates from evil spirits.
From Guinea. Kemoba is ‘grandfather’ in the Malinke area.
The Kennefoli is played during circumcision festivities. It is a tribute to the ones that carry out the circumcisions. It’s much slower than the Söli, which is often preceded by the Kennefoli.
From Guinea. Komo means fetish, don or denu means children. It is the dance of the secrete society Komo. Often played for the mentally ill.
A masked figure from Guinea who protects the bilakoro, or young initiates, in the days before their rite of circumcision.
A masked figure from Guinea who protects the bilakoro, or young initiates, in the days before their rite of circumcision.
From Guinea. Is rhythm of the kassa family, it is played while working in the fields.
From Guinea. A dance variation of the Konkoba. It is rhythm of the kassa family, it is played while working in the fields.
From Guinea. A very faswt dance variation of the Konkoba, in 4 beats, played in ballets. It is rhythm of the kassa family, it is played while working in the fields.

From Guinea. It is a rhythm of the kassa family, it is played while working in the fields. The Konkoba Doundoun is also played when the farmers go back to the villages. Another way that the rhythm was used was to honour mighty or rich farmers. There are differences between the regions (Kouroussa, Mandiani, Faranah) in the explanation of the rhythm.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio

From the Ségou region of Mali. The koreduga caste are a part of a separate group within the Bamana tradition. They are easily recognized by their distinctive, slovenly dress. Their role during the celebrations is to make the assembly laugh with their mimicry and acrobatics. Above all else, the koreduga rhythm accompanies the dance of clowns and buffoons. It is danced by both boys and girls.

From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. From the Ségou region of Mali. The koreduga caste are a part of a separate group within the Bamana tradition. They are easily recognized by their distinctive, slovenly dress. Their role during the celebrations is to make the assembly laugh with their mimicry and acrobatics. Above all else, the koreduga rhythm accompanies the dance of clowns and buffoons. It is danced by both boys and girls.
Kono is a creation of Mamady Keïta during his period at the National Ballet of Guinea.
From Guinea. Könönari (Kononari) is a Malinke-rhythm for the women. Könö is a bird in the tree (ri). In the accompanying song people are warned for arrogance because of their beauty.
This rhythm from Guinea gets its name from a wealthy and powerful man. A griot had told him his name would go down in history. This is the result.
This rhythm from Guinea gets its name from a wealthy and powerful man. A griot had told him his name would go down in history. This is the result.

From the Beyla and Kérouané regions in the Guinea forest area. This rhythm is played for the end of the harvest festivities, the return from fishing and during celebration festivities. It is played only on the djembe, as the dunun does not exist in this region. Two small drums are added to the sides of the soloist's djembe. The whole is called a three headed drum. Another drummer keeps up an accompaniment on a small djembe. The kuku has been modified and adapted with dunun and djembe solos for the National Ballet Company.
A Kuku version of Arafan Tourée. From 1959 to 1985 he was their main soloist, composer and musical arranger, as well as selector and trainer of new talent for Les Ballets Africains.

From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. From the Beyla and Kérouané regions in the Guinea forest area. This Guinea rhythm is named after a sacred bush some consider to be a god. People come from all around to praise god and make requests and vows relating to wealth, family and harvesting.

Kurunen Kun’Do means peak of a little mountain. The rhythm is played slowly, but because of the high density of the bass drums there is a good groove. The song that goes with it expresses the importance to not forget where you come from, always remember your roots and your family, especially when you have reached a top of a mountain.

Originating in the Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso ( Bobo Dioulasso ). This rhythm is played during festivities towards the end of Ramadan, the 27th night. It is the last big fling for the young girls who will be married the following year.

From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. Originating in the Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso ( Bobo Dioulasso ). This rhythm is played during festivities towards the end of Ramadan, the 27th night. It is the last big fling for the young girls who will be married the following year.

A Guinea rhythm originally from the Kouyate lineage of Mali. It has origins on the balaphone, but it's commonly accompanied by doun douns and djembe. It is played for and by the djeli to thank the gods for creating the djeli caste.
Lambé is a popular rhythm that is related to Djagbé and that is played during joyful festivities
Lengjen (Lingjin) comes from Senegal, some specify this to the Casamance region.

A rhythm created to celebrate Guinea's independence from France. During the days that Guinea got it’s independance from France (1958) one Ballet-performance-group that competed at the National Festival called itself Ballet Liberté. It is a transformed Tiriba.

A rhythm created to celebrate Guinea's independence from France. During the days that Guinea got it’s independance from France (1958) one Ballet-performance-group that competed at the National Festival called itself Ballet Liberté. It is a transformed Djolé.
Originating from the Faranah region in northeast Guinea, lolo is a rhythm about consulting the stars for advice when having a problem.
From the region of Guinea-Bassa is a Sousou rhythm that is normally played fast.
From the region of Guinea-Bassa is a Sousou rhythm that is normally played fast.

From the ethnic group, originating in the Kankaba region of Mali ( Bamaka circle ). The madan is played at the end of the harvest to celebrate plenty and prosperity. It is also played as a welcome during popular festivities.

From the ethnic group, originating in the Kankaba region of Mali ( Bamaka circle ). The madan is played at the end of the harvest to celebrate plenty and prosperity. It is also played as a welcome during popular festivities.

A lighthearted courting rhythm from Guinea whereby young girls get the opportunity to express their love and admiration to the young boys. It is a rhythm of flirtation and seduction. It is often played in conjunction with Yancadi.

A lighthearted courting rhythm from Guinea whereby young girls get the opportunity to express their love and admiration to the young boys. It is a rhythm of flirtation and seduction. It is often played in conjunction with Yancadi.
Makende (Makinde) is a Sousou rhythm from Guinea that is played to promote healing in sick (old) men.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio

A Guinea rhythm that deals with the perils of greed and jealousy. Dressed in goubas and embroided shirts, male and female dancers could express their beauty, while dancing in two circles (men in outer circle, women in inner circle).
This rhythm from Mali is played mostly by women during popular celebrations.
This rhythm from Mali is played mostly by women during popular celebrations.

Matadi is the name of an old woman who is limited by her disabilities. The story tells us that when Matadi was young (her sunny time) she could dance enthusiastically to this rhythm, which now bears her name.

From the book Westafrikanische Djemberhythmen of Stephan Rigert. Originates from the area between the Siguiri and Mendiana regions in Guinea and the Kayes region in Mali. Every village within these regions has a Mendiani, a pre-adolescent girl (virgin) who has mastered the dance of Mendiani. The rhythm is played to test the skills of the dancers. The best dancer is then initiated into the secret society of Mendiani, which consists of previous Mendiani.

Originates from the area between the Siguiri and Mendiana regions in Guinea and the Kayes region in Mali. Every village within these regions has a Mendiani, a pre-adolescent girl (virgin) who has mastered the dance of Mendiani. The rhythm is played to test the skills of the dancers. The best dancer is then initiated into the secret society of Mendiani, which consists of previous Mendiani.

Menie (Menie) is a Malinke rhythm from Guinea that used to be played on the occasion of the birth of a child, or more specific: on the day that a name is given to the child (about one week after it´s been born).
Mola is a Malinke dance for youngsters to dance before the circumcision. The circumstances determine whether it is played for boy’s or girls.
Meaning of the song: every day people are born and every day people die. Beautiful and bad things happen all the time. There is no need for envy.
A Guinea rhythm played only for very special occasions such as the return of a special person who has not been seen in many years.
This Soli is played in the Kankan and Kouroussa regions of Guinea and is used for cultivation rather than circumcision.

This rhythm from Guinea refers to an exchange between the older people, the Baratingi, and the younger people, the Baradogono. The Baratingi consider themselves to be the owners of the Bara. This dance occurs when they are challenged by the Baradogono.
A sorcerers rhythm from the Bambara (or Bamana) people of the Wassolon region of Mali
A sorcerers rhythm from the Bambara (or Bamana) people of the Wassolon region of Mali
Noumou (Numun) is the Malinke rhythm of the blacksmiths.

This rhythm belongs to the Dunumba family; ‘The dance of the strong men’. Even more specifically, N’Fa Kaba is referred to as the long Donaba. The story is about a man named Kaba, who for a long time was known as the best dancer and strongest wrestler. The elderly advised him to give up dancing and wrestling and pass the baton to the younger generation. He then goes on a long journey and comes back as a wise marabout. The song praises this transition and is sung in honour of Kaba.
N’Goron is a rhythm of the Senufo that live in Ivory Coast and Burkina Faso. It accompanies a dance that marks the end of the virginity of the girls.
by Stefano Fratini Attanasio
Panthère (Panther, Panther) is the dance of the animals. This rhythm is usually played quickly and often followed by fast Soli.
A rhythm that evolved in South America. However, it is played a lot in many occasions and variations in West Africa.

Saa is a Malinke rhythm from the Faranah region. The word means snake, but also mentally immature person. Like Kennefoli it’ s a rhythm that is played by the man who performs the circumcisions to boys (often the blacksmith). He also dances to the rhythm.
A rhythm from Guinea created for djembe, but inspired from the music of the Sabar from Senegal.
From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. A rhythm from Guinea created for djembe, but inspired from the music of the Sabar from Senegal.
Famudu seminar
Senefoli, a Malinke rhythm, means farming rhythm: sene (farming) and foli (rhythm). A dance to do at the occasion of harvesting the rice.
Senefoli, a Malinke rhythm, means farming rhythm: sene (farming) and foli (rhythm). A dance to do at the occasion of harvesting the rice.
Senefoli, a Malinke rhythm, means farming rhythm: sene (farming) and foli (rhythm). A dance to do at the occasion of harvesting the rice.

Famoudou Konate composed this rhythm to match a song. Sila means ‘the road”. Children have played in the forest all day. They have caught and roasted mice. But when the darkness comes in they are lost. One of the children knows an uplifting song. During the song, the hand is expelled one side or the other. The last time is of course the right side.
Payed for celebrations in the villages of Nalu, near the Boké region of Guinea.

The day before the celebrations for the end of the ramadan, groups of youngsters gather together in their huts. All night lang the talk, make jokes and they challenge each other. During the night, the Kondenba, the keeper of the Konden-mask, comes around the hut and the Konden rhythm is played. In the morning Sirankuruni is sung. They go to the village square where the boys whip each other.

A song of praise from Guinea, it is played for nobles who have shown their worth in battle. Originating in the Kouroussa, Kankan, and Faranah regions of upper Guinea. This rhythm goes back to the time of King Samory. At that time, sofa was played only for war parades to glorify kings and their victories. The djembe was accompanied by the bolon and dunun.

From the Mopti region of Mali. Traditionally, this rhythm is played with three bongolo and a bara. It celebrates plenty at the end of the fishing season. Currently, the sogolon is played with the djembe in the Bamako district, during popular celebrations and festivities.

Originates from the Faranah region in Guinea. In a traditional context it is played for and danced by the uninitiated during the months preceding the male rite of circumcision. The Bilakoro, boys who will be circumcised, have their heads shaved and receive gifts while Soko is played.

A Guinea rhythm played throughout the Malinka country. The soli is specifically for all circumcision or excision events. Circumcision is a ritual operation performed when boys are about seven years old. When the family councils in a given village have posted the list of candidates to be promoted that year and set the date of the ceremonies, the preparations can begin. The mothers prepare the traditional dress. The fathers proceed with consultations to elect the wise man who will watch over the circumcised boys throughout their initiation, which lasts four weeks. In the public gathering area, singing and drums call people to dance the very popular solisi or furasi. In Mali, this rhythm is also called suku or fura.

From the Kankan and Kouroussa regions of Guinea Soli-lent (slow Soli) is a Malinke-rhythm that was played before, during and after initiation rituals; especially during the last three days before initiation. Everybody dances on this slow rhytm. Nowadays is played often, also at other party’s where is speculated on the furtility of this marriage.

Solibasi is an very old version of Soli. It is not played very often these days in Guinea. It belongs to the rhythm family of boy’s circumcision rituals. The rhythm is played by almost no interruption from evening to morning before circumcision to ensure that the boys stay awake and to prepare them emotionally for the event.

From the book West Afrikaanse Percussie of Ponda O' Brian. The rhythm is from Guinea. Refers to a red panther that is in charge of protecting the Bilakoro, or young boys, and the sounkoundoun, the young girls, in the days preceding circumcision.
A rhythm from Guinea.

From the coastal region of Guinea. It is a rhythm danced in full moonlight by young girls out of respect for their mothers. The Sorsornet is a mask from the Baga-people from Boke. The mask protects the village but is kept outside the village in the forest. Someone can make an appeal on the mask because of big problems. A priest can go and get the mask and then Sorsornet is played and the mask goes around the village.

From the the Kayes region of Mali . This very popular rhythm is believed to date back to the pre-colonial era. At that time, in the village of Sagabari , there was a pretty young girl named Sunu Mamady (her father had the same name). Everyone loved her, and her qualities as a dancer were greatly appreciated. No festivity could take place without her participation. This rhythm was created in her honor by a djembefola troupe from her village. The dance is played to celebrate good harvests. It is a moment for young girls to demonstrate their grace and beauty, sometimes even their provocativeness and for young boys, especially in the Kaarta circle , to demonstrate their strength and vigor and show their acrobatic prowess.

Originating in the Boké region of lower Guinea. Traditionally the tiriba is not played on the djembe but on smaller drums made of stretched deerskin with wooden corners. It is played for circumcisions and also during the medicine men's important festivities and ceremonies.

Originates from northeast Guinea. Toro is a Malinke rhythm from the Siguiri region in Guinea was originally played after the initiation of boys; a group of boys has been together for three months (‘on camp’) and have learned all the rules and practices of life as an adult (including recognizing botany and bird sounds). Some time after the circumcision, a big fire is made and the rhythm is played; formerly played without djembé ‘s, but with the wasssamba.
Tuba is a djembé rhythm from Guinea developed by Arafan Touré. He is a member of the Sousou ethnic group and for many years he was the creative director of the Ballet de Guinée.
A rhythm from Mali similar to N'Gri

Wolesedon (Wolosedon, Wolosodan, Djondon, Jondon, Djonfoli) comes from the Kayes region of Mali. It means ‘Dance of the Woloso’, dance of the slaves. Wolesedon concerns the slaves who used to serve at the royal courts of the Mandinka Kings and their families. The dance shows the family honour and solidarity.

From Guinea. A lighthearted courting rhythm whereby young girls get the opportunity to express their love and admiration to the young boys. It is a rhythm of flirtation and seduction. It is often played in conjunction with Makru.

A rhythm from Senegal played for celebrations, marriages and initiations. It has become very popular in Guinea and is played for celebrations.

Originates from the Zuénoula region of Ivory Coast. It is usually played to accompany funeral rites. A masked figure, called the Zawouli, represents evil. Today it has evolved into a celebration dance for the people and is often played in conjunction with Coucou or Diansa.
